newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU wants semiconductor deal linked to ITA.
newsitem.headline: EU wants semiconductor deal linked to ITA.

text.p: The European Union, accused by Washington of dragging its feet on an International Technology Agreement (ITA), wants to be included in the U.S.-Japan semiconductor alliance before moving ahead.

EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, on Monday preparing for this week's Quadrilateral meeting in Seattle, Washington, won support for this strategy during an informal meeting of the 15-nation bloc's trade ministers in Dublin last week.
Brittan warned there could be no progress on an ITA unless steps are taken to include the EU in a semiconductor deal signed in July by the United States and Japan after long negotiations.

The Quad meeting, which brings together the trade ministers of Canada, the United States, Japan and the EU, this Thursday to Saturday, is expected to focus on an ITA, which which aims to reduce tariffs and other barriers on a wide range of products including semiconductors, computer hardware and software as well as telephone equipment.
It has been on the drawing board since the World Trade Organisation took over from the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade last year.
The WTO seeks to introduce a global rules-based system of trade instead of the previous rash of bilateral and multilateral agreements that emerged during the computer industry boom of the 1980s.
On Friday, U.S. acting trade representative Charlene Barshefsky said an ITA was impossible without Europe's participation.

"Europe needs to demonstrate leadership here," Barshefsky told reporters on Friday in a briefing ahead of the quad meeting. "(But) Europe seems to be backing away now, which would be very dissappointing."
Privately, U.S. and industry officlas say they are unsure of Europe's motives in moving away from a deal, saying it could be a bargaining position or reflect division within the EU.
But EU officials insist there is no division, and Brittan says he wants an ITA as much as anyone. Sources say, however, he is still fuming at being excluded from July's U.S-Japan semiconductor deal.

The deal puts responsibility for monitoring semiconductor sales between those countries on the industry itself. It also guarantees the United States will continue to enjoy at least 19 percent of Japan's domestic market.
Although Brittan has described the alliance as "toothless", he is nevertheless concerned European chip producers have corenered a mere three percent of the Japanese market.
Japan was reluctant to sign any deal, saying its market was already operating freely with nearly 30 percent of chip sales from foreign producers.

Analysts say Barshefsky, knowing the U.S. is producing at full capacity has more than 20 percent of the market anyway, was desperate for a deal to formally include in president Bill Clinton's relection campaign.

Washington and Tokyo have tried to include the EU, as well as emerging chip produces such as South Korea and Taiwan, in the deal by promising to establish a Global Governmental Forum along WTO lines, but Brittan is believed to want a more formal trilateral participation.

But, analysts say, the EU is expecting something for nothing. They note the EU still has a seven percent tariff on semiconductor imports -- the United States and Japan have bilaterally scrapped theirs -- and argue also that European manufacturers are just not competitive enough.
